lessons.title: Receiving animals at the abattoir
lessons.html:
Receiving animals at the abattoir

Ante mortem means before death. This unit is about how you handle live cattle, sheep, goats and pigs from the time the truck arrives until they go to the stunning box.

When the truck arrives

  1. Check that the papers come with the animals. The papers show where the animals come from and who owns them.
  2. Count the animals as they come off the truck. The number must match the papers.
  3. Look at each animal as it walks off. Is it lame? Is it hurt? Is it sick or weak?
  4. Tell your supervisor about any animal that is down, hurt or looks sick. Do not hide it.

Off-loading

  • Use the ramp. Never make animals jump down from the truck.
  • Let the animals walk at their own speed.
  • Keep the ramp clean and not slippery.
  • An animal that cannot walk must not be dragged. Call your supervisor. It will be handled according to the abattoir's procedure.

In the pens (lairage)

  • Put animals from the same group together. Do not mix strange bulls or boars, because they fight.
  • Do not put too many animals in one pen. Every animal must be able to lie down.
  • Make sure there is clean drinking water in every pen.
  • Keep sick or hurt animals in a separate pen for the meat inspector to look at.

The meat inspector checks the live animals before slaughter. This is the ante mortem inspection. Only animals that pass may go to slaughter. Your job is to help by keeping the animals calm, clean and in the right pens, with the pen numbers and records correct.

lessons.title: Moving animals calmly and safely
lessons.html:
Moving animals calmly and safely

Calm animals are safer for you, and they give better meat. Stressed animals bruise, and bruised meat must be cut away and thrown out. Stress before slaughter can also make the meat dark and poor quality.

How animals see and move

  • Animals see well to the sides but not right behind them. Do not stand in the blind spot behind an animal.
  • Animals move forward when you step behind their shoulder, and stop or turn back when you step in front of it.
  • Animals do not like shadows, loud noise, shiny things or flapping cloth in the race. Look for these and remove them.
  • Animals follow each other. Move small groups, not one animal alone.

What to use

  • Use a flag, a paddle or a rattle to guide animals.
  • Use your voice quietly. Do not shout or whistle loudly.

What you must never do

  • Never hit, kick or twist the tail of an animal.
  • Never use sticks with nails, or poke the eyes or private parts.
  • Never use an electric prodder on calves, sheep or goats, or on the face of any animal. Use it only where your abattoir allows it, and only on large animals that refuse to move.
  • Never lift a sheep by its wool or legs.

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty to animals a crime. Cruel handling can lead to a fine, jail, and losing your job.

Your own safety

  • Wear safety boots.
  • Always know where your escape route is in the pen.
  • Never get into a pen with an angry bull or a sow with piglets.
  • Work with a partner when moving cattle.

Key points

  • Count the animals and check the papers when they arrive.
  • Report any sick, hurt or downer animal to your supervisor.
  • Every pen needs clean water and enough space.
  • Move animals quietly with a flag or paddle, never by hitting them.
  • Cruelty is against the law and spoils the meat.
